title: By whose grace
hookLine: jih prasaad: by whose grace you eat fine foods and wear fine clothes, remember Him

cards: Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad.
Read ashtpadi six aloud and those two words come round again and again, at the start of line after line, like a drum keeping time under a song. By whose grace.
Each time, a different gift follows, and the gifts in the first stanza are surprisingly ordinary for a sacred text. Not visions. Not miracles.

teach.h: JIH: BY WHOSE. PRASAAD: FREE GIFT.
teach.b: Jih means by whom, by whose. Prasaad, you met yesterday: grace, a gift freely given.

In the gurdwara, the sweet offering given into cupped hands at the end of a service is called karah prashad, and today's word can be heard in its name. So jih prasaad: by whose free gift. The first stanza goes like this.

By whose grace you eat the thirty-six delicacies, a phrase read as every kind of fine food, keep that Master in your mind. By whose grace you put fragrance on your body, remembering Him you reach the highest state.
By whose grace you live in a house of comfort, meditate on Him always. And the next stanza picks up the clothes: by whose grace you wear silks and fine cloth, why abandon Him and cling to another?
Every line has two halves. First, a gift you can taste, smell or touch.
Then a turning: remember, keep in mind, don't forget. Guru Arjan doesn't ask anyone to give up the meal or the shirt.
He asks for the meal to become a reminder.
It's the same move as the ten things, made smaller and more frequent: not once a year at a feast, but every time you sit down to eat.

how: Many Sikhs remember Waheguru before eating, and in the gurdwara karah prashad is received in cupped hands as a gift of grace; ashtpadi six's 'jih prasaad' refrain is read as part of Sukhmani Sahib.

o: a prayer asking God for a good meal
by whose grace, the refrain before each gift
a sweet offering handed out at the gurdwara

games.q: by whose grace — tap the pairs.
p: the sweet offering in cupped hands

s: ashtpadi six asks people to give up fine food and clothes
it asks for each gift to become a reminder of the Giver.
'jih prasaad' comes round again and again in ashtpadi six
like a drum: by whose grace, by whose grace.
each line pairs a gift with a turning toward the Giver
a gift you can taste or touch, then: remember Him.

games.q: a full plate is in front of you. by ashtpadi six, what's the move?
o: push it away to prove you don't need it.
eat, and let the meal turn your mind to the Giver.
eat fast and get on with the day.
games.why: by whose grace you eat the thirty-six delicacies, keep that Master in your mind: the meal becomes a reminder.

practice: Picture the next thing you'll eat, a plate, a sandwich, a cup of tea, and see where it came from: a field, a farmer, a truck, a shop, someone's hands. Then let the drumbeat come: jih prasaad, by whose grace.
If you pray, let that be your thanks; if you don't, let it be a moment of noticing that none of it began with you.

wordCard.voice: Jih prasaad. By whose grace: the refrain of ashtpadi six, set before every ordinary gift.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jih prasaad, by whose grace; the refrain of Sukhmani's sixth ashtpadi.

carryVoice: Your line: by his grace, this meal. Grace, set at the table. Day four hundred fifty-nine, done.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
